back: A group of individuals of a given species, sharing or competing for similar resources in a well-defined geographical area, potentially interbreeding.
Per capita number of births during a given period added to the population.
Per capita number of deaths during a given period in the population.
The proportion of males and females in a population (e.g. 60% female, 40% male).
Graphical representation of the age distribution of a population; shape indicates growing, stable or declining status.
Size of a population; can be numbers, biomass or per cent cover depending on the species.
B increases density, D decreases density.
I increases density (dominates early colonisation), E decreases it.
r = b - d; governs exponential growth dN/dt = rN.
Unlimited resources; J-shaped curve; N_t = N_0 e^(rt).
Maximum population a given habitat can support.
Limited resources; sigmoid curve; dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K).
One species (predator) benefits, the other (prey) is harmed; transfers energy to higher trophic levels.
Both species suffer reduced fitness from shared limiting resources.
Two closely related species competing for the same limiting resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the inferior one is eliminated.
Coexistence mechanism: competing species avoid overlap by using different times/foraging patterns.
Parasite benefits at host's expense; ectoparasites (surface) vs endoparasites (inside body).
One species benefits; other unaffected (orchid on mango, cattle egret with cattle, clown fish with anemone).
Both species benefit (lichens, mycorrhizae, fig-wasp, orchids-bees).
One species is harmed; the other is unaffected.
